title: Crystallographic imperfections and exotic superconductivity of UBe$_{13}$
authors: Andreas Leithe-Jasper, Markus König, Yusei Shimizu, Konstantin Semeniuk, Primož Koželj, Mitja Krnel, Paul Simon, Wilder Carrillo-Cabrera, Nazar Zaremba, Marcel Naumann, Ulrich Burkhardt, Thomas Doert, Yurii Prots, Alfred Amon, Elena Gati, Matthias Vojta, Yuri Grin, Elena Hassinger, Eteri Svanidze
abstract: The symmetry of the superconducting gap is related to the symmetry of the crystal structure. In unconventional superconductors, big changes of the critical temperature, critical field or even the gap structure can happen even for small perturbations of the lattice. In this letter, we use microstructuring to study aluminium-free crystals of UBe$_{13}$ which are expected to be closer to "perfect" material than previously studied aluminium-grown single crystals. We compare the effect of minuscule imperfections on the value of the critical temperature and critical field, which, in the case of UBe$_{13}$, has drastic effects, supporting its unconventional nature. We conjecture that this likely arises from the oxidation state of uranium, which is sensitive to its crystal environment. Our findings suggests that uranium-based materials provide not only an excellent reservoir of new unconventional phenomena, but also a way to identify the gap symmetry of unconventional superconductors.
summary: This work examines the relationship between crystal structure and exotic superconductivity in UBe13. By using microstructuring, the authors demonstrate that even minuscule imperfections, such as Be vacancies, cause drastic changes in the superconducting critical temperature. This highlights the extreme structural sensitivity of unconventional superconductors and suggests that material perfection is crucial for understanding their fundamental physics.
main_problem: The study investigates how minute crystallographic imperfections affect the exotic superconductivity observed in UBe13, a heavy-fermion superconductor.
main_result: The critical temperature (Tc) of UBe13 is extremely sensitive to Be vacancies, showing drastic changes with minor lattice parameter shifts, suggesting the superconducting gap symmetry is highly dependent on the crystal environment.
method: The research employs microstructuring techniques to isolate single crystallites and measures superconducting properties (Tc, upper critical field) alongside structural characterization (EBSD, TEM).
model_or_system: The physical system is UBe13, a uranium-based unconventional superconductor, whose properties are studied across various stoichiometric variants (UBe13-x) and impurity-doped forms (UBe13-xAl_x).
key_observables: Critical temperature (Tc), upper critical field (Hc2), lattice parameter (a), and electrical resistivity (r(T)).
important_parameters: Lattice parameter changes ($\sim 0.006\%$ causing $28\%$ change in Tc); Be deficiency concentration ($x$); Temperature range (down to 60 mK).
main_assumptions: The observed sensitivity is attributed to the oxidation state of uranium being highly sensitive to its local crystal environment, and that strain from secondary phases is insufficient to explain the observed Tc shifts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationship between Tc and lattice parameter for various compounds, show microstructural analysis (EBSD/TEM), and present resistivity/specific heat data comparing samples with different levels of structural disorder.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the link between crystal symmetry and superconducting gap symmetry, detailing microstructural characterization, quantifying the extreme sensitivity of Tc to Be deficiency, and finally comparing these findings with theoretical expectations for unconventional superconductors.
why_interesting: The extreme sensitivity of the superconducting state to atomic-scale disorder provides a tangible experimental realization of how local structural perturbations can dramatically alter complex quantum many-body ground states, which is relevant to understanding disorder effects in quantum materials.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Interplay of chemistry and physics in U1−yThyBe13−xAlx: superconductivity as a function of structural disorder, as reflected by the value of Tc (vertical axis) vs. lattice parameter a (horizontal axis). Three distinct regions exist, representing three different materials UBe13−x (red, present study), UBe13−xAlx (orange [8]), and U1−yThyBe13 (yellow [9, 10]) – all showing superconductivity, albeit of different character. In some cases, imperfections on the atomic scale can only be seen by means of transmission electron microscopy (insets).

Figure 2. Extraction of intrinsic electrical resistivity of UBe13−x: (a) Electron back-scatter diffraction is used to estimate grain size. (b) and (c): Inclusions of U (light gray) or Be (dark gray) secondary phases is easily recognizable in the lamellae, extracted from polycrystalline material. (d) and (e): Micro-scale devices, fabricated from polycrystalline samples. The current flow is left to right, which means that several voltage pairs avoid inclusions of U or Be – this allows to capture the intrinsic resistivity of UBe13−x. (f) and (g): A piece from the same device is then used to pinpoint defects on the atomic scale by means of transmission electron microscopy.

Figure 3. Intrinsic superconductivity of UBe13−x: (a) and (b) Micro-scale resistivity reveals that the superconducting transition temperature of UBe13−x is changing by almost 30%, depending on whether polycrystalline material is growing from U (red) or Be (green) excess. For all samples, only one superconducting anomaly is observed, with its position being different for different starting U:Be ratios. (c) The specific heat data follow the same trend. (d) All of the UBe13−x grains within a given sample have the same composition, given the agreement between the value of Tc extracted from the micro-scale (triangles, resistivity) and bulk (circles, specific heat) data.
